    Oral Exam 2 Information#

    Last updated: November 26, 2026.

    Scheduling and exam format#

    Oral exam 2 appointments take place from Wednesday, December 2, through finals week. I will circulate a calendar sign-up link.

    When you arrive for the exam, you will be given a choice of two topics from the list below. You will select one topic and have up to 40 minutes to prepare your exposition. This preparation period is closed book: you may not use notes, books, or other resources.

    After the preparation period, you will have a discussion at the board of around 40 minutes (not timed). You may consult any notes you produced during your preparation time.

    During the board discussion, you should be prepared to:

    • give a coherent overview of the selected topic and explain how its main ideas fit together;

    • state definitions and mathematical statements precisely;

    • present the central proofs at the level of their overall structure;

    • supply detailed arguments for individual steps when asked; and

    • respond to questions about hypotheses, examples, counterexamples, and connections among the results.

    A presentation does not have to be flawless to earn full marks. The goal is to demonstrate that you have understood the topic and can think about it at the board. Tips or suggestions may be provided if you get stuck. If you are receptive to suggestions and recover from a temporary hesitation, you can still earn full marks.

    Example grading rubric#

    The exam will be assessed holistically. The following descriptions illustrate the level of performance associated with each score range.

    • 90–100%: Demonstrates a strong and connected understanding of the topic. Definitions and statements are precise when requested, the main proof ideas are correct, and detailed arguments are supplied with only minor omissions or errors. Responds thoughtfully to questions and can use a tip to recover from hesitation. The presentation need not be perfect.

    • 80–89%: Demonstrates good understanding of the main ideas and proof structure. Most definitions and statements are accurate, but there are some gaps, imprecisions, or errors of substance. Responds productively to questions and suggestions, though some issues remain unresolved.

    • 70–79%: Demonstrates substantial but incomplete understanding. Can explain several central ideas and parts of the proofs, but important definitions, hypotheses, connections, or proof steps are missing or incorrect. Follow-up questions reveal uneven command of the topic. Can carry out at least one technical proof to completion.

    • 60–69%: Demonstrates limited understanding. Can state some relevant definitions or results and make partial progress on proofs, but the overall structure is unclear or contains errors. Substantial prompting is needed to proceed.

    • 50–59%: Demonstrates limited understanding. Some relevant facts are recalled, but central definitions, statements, and proof ideas are seriously incomplete or inaccurate. Makes little progress even with significant guidance.

    • Below 50%: Does not yet demonstrate a workable understanding of the selected topic.

    Topics#

    Status: The topic list is final.

    Unless an item is explicitly marked statement only, you should be able to give precise definitions and prove both the statement and auxiliary facts for the result. This applies to all mentioned facts: theorems, propositions, lemmata, or corollaries, and examples.

    Topic 5: Product measures and Tonelli’s theorem#

    In this topic, proofs are to be carried out only for finite measures: and . You should know the statements for -finite measures.

    1. Definitions. Measurable rectangles; the product -algebra , the smallest -algebra containing all measurable rectangles; sections of sets and functions; the product outer measure and the product measure; -finiteness.

    2. Existence of the product measure. Give the construction and check each of the following properties.

      • The cost of a measurable rectangle depends only on the set .

      • The product outer measure is the outer measure generated by this cost, so it is an outer measure (Outer Measures).

      • The cost is -subadditive on rectangles: if , then . Prove this using characteristic functions: prove and integrate in .

      • The outer measure extends the cost: (extension property, Outer Measures).

      • Measurable rectangles satisfy the Carathéodory criterion: cut each rectangle of a cover into pieces.

      • The Carathéodory measurable sets form a -algebra, which therefore contains , and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a measure (Carathéodory Measurability). These facts may be quoted.

    3. Lebesgue measure. Explain why on Borel sets: the two measures agree on open rectangles, which generate the Borel sets, and the coincidence criterion for -finite measures applies. The identity may be used without proof.

    4. Uniqueness. Prove uniqueness of the product measure for finite and , for example using the coincidence criterion, which follows from Dynkin’s theorem. State the -finite version, which follows from the coincidence criterion for -finite measures, and state that uniqueness can fail without -finiteness.

    5. Statement of Tonelli’s theorem. State Tonelli’s theorem precisely for -finite measures, with its hypotheses and all its conclusions, including measurability of the sections and of the inner integrals.

    6. Tonelli’s theorem for finite measures. Define the Tonelli class, which includes measurability of sections, prove that it is a -system, and use Dynkin’s theorem to prove the result for indicator functions. Extend it to simple and then to non-negative measurable functions. Identify where finiteness is used.

    7. Minkowski’s integral inequality. For -finite and , , and an -measurable , explain why both sides are defined and prove that using Tonelli’s theorem, Hölder’s inequality, and the testing property of norms, which may be quoted.

    Course notes: Product -algebras and Product Measures; Tonelli’s Theorem.
